subtype: Business traveller and a tired mind [Observer]
passage: Mehak noticed it the moment Manoj walked into the spice-packing unit at Kumily. He had flown back from a trade fair in Germany the night before and caught the early bus up the ghat. At the morning meeting he snapped at the foreman over a small spelling slip on a label, then dozed off with his chin on his hand while the cardamom prices were being read out. When a trader from Bodi arrived wanting a quick yes on a large order, Mehak stepped in. 'Sir only got back yesterday. Can we give you an answer on Wednesday?' The trader shrugged and agreed. At lunch Mehak slid a glass of lime juice across the table. 'Go home early, sir. The order will keep.' Manoj rubbed his eyes and, for once, did not argue.

qa.q: What did Manoj do while the cardamom prices were being read out?
qa.a: He dozed off with his chin on his hand.

qa.q: What was Mehak thinking when the trader wanted a quick yes?
qa.a: Mehak was worried that Manoj, worn out from the long trip, might misjudge a large order, so stepped in to buy time.

qa.q: Why was asking for an answer on Wednesday a fair and practical choice?
qa.a: It gave Manoj a few days to recover from the trip before a big decision, without refusing the trader.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt when Mehak told him to go home early?
qa.a: He probably felt tired and a little relieved, too worn out to argue, and perhaps grateful that someone had noticed.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing someone back from a long trip being irritable and dozing in a meeting, and fairly delaying a crucial decision to give time to adjust.

subtype: Business traveller and a tired mind [Observer]
passage: Javier landed in Madrid from Singapore at six on Monday morning and was at his desk by nine, proud of it. Mei, who sat opposite, watched him over her monitor. He read the same email three times, snapped at the intern about a stapler, and in the ten o'clock meeting his chin sank twice. When the manager asked him to sign off the new supplier contract, Javier said, 'Sure, fine, whatever.' Mei winced. After the meeting she caught the manager in the corridor. 'He's been awake for thirty hours. Can the contract wait till Wednesday?' The manager agreed. Mei sent Javier home at two with a sticky note: 'Sleep. The contract will still be here.'

qa.q: What did Mei write on the sticky note?
qa.a: 'Sleep. The contract will still be here.'

qa.q: Why did Mei wince when Javier said 'Sure, fine, whatever'?
qa.a: She felt worried that Javier, exhausted and foggy from the flight, was about to agree to a big contract without really thinking.

qa.q: What was fair and practical about Mei's move?
qa.a: She asked for the contract to wait until Wednesday and sent Javier home, giving him time to adjust before an important decision.

qa.q: How might Javier have seen his own Monday?
qa.a: He probably felt proud of coming straight to work, not noticing how tired and irritable he had become.

grounding: A colleague notices a jet-lagged coworker dozing and snapping and gets a crucial decision postponed.

subtype: Business traveller and a tired mind [Observer]
passage: The engineering college staff room was buzzing about the exam timetable. Arohi had flown back from a conference in Chicago the night before and insisted on coming in. Ganga, the department coordinator, noticed her yawning into her sleeve, then arguing sharply with the lab assistant over a missing file that turned out to be in her own bag. When the head of department asked Arohi to finalise the question-paper allocation that afternoon, Ganga cut in gently. 'She has half a day of time difference in her head. Let's give her tomorrow off and do the allocation on Thursday.' Arohi opened her mouth to protest, then laughed tiredly. 'Thursday,' she agreed.

qa.q: Where was the missing file?
qa.a: In Arohi's own bag.

qa.q: What was Ganga worried about when Arohi was asked to finalise the allocation?
qa.a: Ganga felt concerned that a tired, jet-lagged Arohi would make poor judgments on something important that afternoon.

qa.q: Why was Ganga's suggestion fair and practical?
qa.a: It gave Arohi a day to adjust and moved the crucial allocation to Thursday, when she could think clearly.

qa.q: How might Arohi have felt when Ganga suggested a day off?
qa.a: Arohi may have felt a flash of pride and wanted to protest, then relief, laughing tiredly as she agreed.

grounding: A coordinator sees a jet-lagged colleague being irritable and yawning and moves a crucial task to a later day.

subtype: Business traveller and a tired mind [Observer]
passage:
Hi Rafiq,
Welcome back from Nairobi! I know you flew in at dawn yesterday, so please don't read this as a complaint. In the afternoon review you dozed off twice, and when Tanmay asked about the budget sheet you told him it was none of his business. That isn't like you. You also nearly approved the vendor's revised quote, which still has the old freight charges.
I've moved the client call to Friday and told the team you're adjusting. Take tomorrow morning slowly, get some daylight, and let's go through the quote together once you're rested. I'd want someone to do the same for me.
Kiran

qa.q: When did Kiran move the client call to?
qa.a: To Friday.

qa.q: How does Kiran feel about Rafiq's behaviour in the review?
qa.a: Kiran feels concerned rather than annoyed, seeing that the dozing and the sharp reply were unlike Rafiq and likely came from the flight.

qa.q: Why is Kiran's plan for the quote a good one?
qa.a: Going through it together once Rafiq is rested avoids approving the old freight charges by mistake.

qa.q: What might Rafiq feel on reading this email?
qa.a: Rafiq may feel a little embarrassed but relieved, since Kiran explains kindly and has already made room to recover.

grounding: A colleague notices poor judgment and dozing after a long trip and allows time to adjust before key decisions.

subtype: Business traveller and a tired mind [Observer]
passage: Team-lead advice, Kiran? Here's the one story I always tell. I'm Usha, and last year my colleague Gautam flew back from a two-week client visit in Chicago and walked straight into our Monday review. He looked fine, in a crisp shirt. But he nodded off twice during the budget slides, snapped at the intern over a typo, and then agreed to a vendor contract he had argued against for months. I was annoyed at first. Then I felt uneasy, because this wasn't the Gautam I knew. After the meeting I spoke to our manager, and we paused the contract till Thursday. Gautam was embarrassed when he read his own notes later. Now our team has a simple rule: after a long trip, the first day back is for email and sleep, and no big decisions.

qa.q: Where had Gautam been on his client visit?
qa.a: In Chicago, for two weeks.

qa.q: How did Usha's feelings shift during the Monday review?
qa.a: Usha was annoyed at first, then uneasy, sensing this wasn't the Gautam Usha knew.

qa.q: What fair, practical step did Usha take, and what rule came from it?
qa.a: Usha asked the manager to pause the contract till Thursday, and the team now keeps the first day back for email and sleep with no big decisions.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel when he read his own notes later?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed at the poor judgment he had shown while so tired.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing someone back from a long trip dozing, irritable and making a poor judgment, and giving a day to adjust before crucial decisions.
